overview: This file brings together wartime and Occupation-era records concerning the control of correspondence to, from, and within Japan and Japanese-occupied territories. It begins with 1945 International Red Cross arrangements for restricted family messages involving free civilians in Southeast Asia, then documents Allied civil-mail censorship, customs inspection of international parcels, restrictions on scientific manuscripts and atomic-energy research, public inquiries about permissible correspondence, complaints that commercial intelligence obtained from censored mail reached competitors, and State Department requirements for intelligence derived from intercepted communications. Although the supplied file title ends in May 1948, the bundle also contains 1949 material on the dismantling or reduction of Occupation censorship and a later public inquiry about Japanese mail.

subfiles.title: Bern despatch on Red Cross correspondence with uninterned civilians
subfiles.from: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Bern
subfiles.about: Transmits regulations, instructions, and forms for a Japanese-authorized correspondence system serving non-interned civilians in occupied Southeast Asian territories.
subfiles.summary: The American Legation reports receiving the enclosed material from the International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva on January 3, 1945. The Committee prepared it from information supplied by the Japanese Red Cross and had already informed U.S. authorities and the American Red Cross through its Washington delegate.

subfiles.title: Regulations for Far Eastern civilian messages
subfiles.from: International Committee of the Red Cross, based on Japanese Red Cross information
subfiles.to: National Red Cross societies and prospective correspondents
subfiles.about: Sets out the two authorized methods and administrative rules for civilian correspondence with occupied Indonesia, the Philippines, and Burma.
subfiles.summary: Correspondents could either select prescribed English-language family-news phrases or write a message of no more than fifty Japanese kana characters. Messages had to contain identifying particulars for sender and addressee, were transcribed in Tokyo, and were generally limited to one message per person or family every two months. The regulations distinguish this service from the continuing twenty-five-word Red Cross scheme for Japan, Formosa, Korea, occupied China, Shanghai, and Hong Kong.

subfiles.title: Instructions for messages to and from free civilians
subfiles.from: International Committee of the Red Cross
subfiles.to: Users of the Far Eastern message service
subfiles.about: Provides a concise public-facing explanation of the special message system and its routing through Cairo and Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Free civilians in occupied Indonesia, the Philippines, or Burma could use either the prescribed English phrases or a fifty-kana message. The form required personal, occupational, and relationship details, and transmission expenses followed the ordinary civilian-message rules. The page also notes that twenty-five-word postal messages remained in use for Japan, Korea, Formosa, occupied China, Shanghai, and Hong Kong.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Message form and standard phrases
subfiles.from: International Committee of the Red Cross Central Agency for Prisoners of War
subfiles.about: Supplies the blank form for identifying sender and addressee and choosing either a kana message or standard family-news phrases.
subfiles.summary: The form collects names, addresses, nationalities, occupations, relationships, and remarks for both parties. Writers could use a fifty-kana personal message or select from nine informative and six interrogative phrases, but could not combine the two methods. The prescribed phrases cover health, illness, death, birth, marriage, education, employment, living conditions, receipt of communications, and requests for news.

subfiles.title: Routing sheet for Bern despatch No. 10649
subfiles.from: Department of State, Special War Problems Division
subfiles.about: Records departmental routing and filing references for Bern despatch No. 10649 and its transmission via the U.S. naval attaché in Moscow.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies the referenced Bern item as No. 10649 and associates it with decimal file 894.711/1-2045. It contains Special War Problems Division, filing, and routing stamps rather than substantive correspondence.

subfiles.title: ICRC addendum extending the message scheme to Malaya
subfiles.from: International Committee of the Red Cross, Geneva
subfiles.about: Adds Malaya to the civilian correspondence scheme and clarifies delivery and dating of messages.
subfiles.summary: The Committee reports from Tokyo that civilian messages previously forwarded to the Japanese Red Cross for the occupied territories had been sent onward to their addressees. It recommends recording the date a message was written, either under remarks or in a new form field. Fresh Japanese Red Cross information indicated that free civilians in Malaya would also be allowed to exchange family news through the scheme.

subfiles.title: Bern telegram on expanded inter-territorial message service
subfiles.from: American Legation, Bern, signed Huddle
subfiles.about: Reports that the message system had been extended between the southern occupied territories and Japan, occupied China, and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The International Red Cross reported that its Tokyo delegate had learned of the expanded service and that application forms were being sent to delegations in Hong Kong and Shanghai and to the Manchukuo Red Cross. The telegram stresses that correspondence between points located within the southern occupied territories themselves was still not permitted.

subfiles.title: Army transmittal of first Pacific-Asiatic civil-censorship report
subfiles.from: Victor E. Engstrom, Headquarters Army Service Forces
subfiles.to: Department of State, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation; attention Walter E. Jessop
subfiles.about: Forwards the first operating report on civil-censorship activities in Japan and Korea for September 1945.
subfiles.summary: Engstrom sends the State Department a report on early Occupation censorship operations in Japan and Korea. The referenced report was enclosed with the original memorandum but is not reproduced on the supplied page.

subfiles.title: London airgram on British parliamentary question about mail censorship
subfiles.from: U.S. mission in London, coded “LO. DO.”
subfiles.about: Reports a House of Commons exchange concerning U.S. military opening of mail addressed to British subjects through the British Embassy in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Bartlett asked why letters addressed to British subjects at the embassy were opened by the U.S. military civil-mail censor. Mr. Taylor replied that Japanese postal authorities handled all civil mail and had to submit it to Allied censorship, while diplomatic and forces mail were exempt. A copy was sent to the U.S. Political Adviser at SCAP in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting directive on customs inspection of international mail
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits SCAP directives transferring inspection of certain international mail to Japanese customs authorities.
subfiles.summary: The despatch encloses SCAPIN 1756 and detailed Economic and Scientific Section implementation instructions. It notes that inspection would initially take place at Yokohama but that six additional central distribution points were under consideration, allowing parcels to be bagged for destinations other than Yokohama.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1756 directing Japanese customs inspection
subfiles.from: F. M. Levy for the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Japanese Government, through the Central Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Orders the Japanese Government to begin inspecting international parcel post, samples, and small packets on August 15, 1947.
subfiles.summary: The directive places the operation under SCAP instructions, Universal Postal Union rules, and bilateral parcel-post agreements. It also authorizes direct communication between the Ministry of Finance and the appropriate sections of General Headquarters to implement the order.

subfiles.title: Implementation instructions for customs examination of international relief parcels
subfiles.from: Economic and Scientific Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Provides operational rules for Japanese customs control of international parcels, samples, and small packets.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum directs the Customs Bureau to take over examination from the Civil Censorship Detachment on August 15 under Eighth Army surveillance. It specifies permissible relief goods and quantitative limits on cigarettes, cigars, pipe tobacco, and saccharin, and requires extraction of prohibited or excessive items. Customs and police were to monitor suspicious recipients, enforce restrictions on resale or barter, distribute confiscated goods through relief agencies, and maintain detailed records.

subfiles.title: Levi inquiry about publishing a Japanese scientist’s manuscript
subfiles.from: Edward H. Levi
subfiles.about: Asks whether Occupation regulations prevented a Japanese scientist from submitting an article to an American scientific journal.
subfiles.summary: Levi recounts that a University of Chicago atomic scientist and journal editor had invited an unknown Japanese correspondent to submit a promising article. The Japanese scientist replied that he was not permitted to do so and was having difficulty obtaining authorization. Levi asks whether this resulted from regulations imposed by the American Occupation authority.

subfiles.title: Schuler memorandum on Japanese scientific manuscripts and atomic-energy controls
subfiles.from: Frank A. Schuler Jr.
subfiles.about: Suggests that the manuscript was probably restricted by the Far Eastern Commission’s atomic-energy directive.
subfiles.summary: Schuler reasons that the Japanese scientist may have been working in nuclear physics and therefore subject to FEC 024/7, which prohibited Japanese atomic-energy research and related activity. He adds that manuscripts in other fields could be published abroad if routed through SCAP and the Department of the Army.

subfiles.title: Martin reply to Levi on mailing and censoring scientific manuscripts
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin
subfiles.about: Explains the postal and censorship procedures governing efforts by Japanese nationals to publish manuscripts abroad.
subfiles.summary: Martin states that Japanese nationals were not allowed to send manuscripts outside Japan under ordinary postal regulations. SCAP might agree to transmit a manuscript on a scientist’s behalf, but would censor it. Publication could still be refused if the work concerned atomic energy, owing to the Far Eastern Commission’s prohibition on Japanese activity in that field.

subfiles.title: Despatch on additional Japanese customs inspection offices
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a SCAP memorandum announcing additional customs offices for international mail.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Political Adviser refers to the August despatch on Japanese customs inspection and forwards five copies of a November 11 memorandum. The enclosure was intended to help diplomatic missions inform their national postal administrations about the new Japanese inspection arrangements.

subfiles.title: SCAP memorandum establishing regional customs-mail offices
subfiles.from: F. M. Levy for the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Diplomatic missions in Japan and the Soviet member of the Allied Council for Japan
subfiles.about: Announces six customs inspection offices and assigns Japanese prefectures to each office for the sorting of foreign parcel mail.
subfiles.summary: Customs offices at Moji, Nagasaki, Osaka, Shimonoseki, Tokyo, and Yokohama were to inspect parcel post, samples, and small packets from November 15. Foreign postal administrations were asked to bag mail by groups of destination prefectures and label the sacks for the appropriate inspection office. The sacks could nevertheless enter Japan through any port.

subfiles.title: Crawford inquiry about correspondence with Japan
subfiles.from: S. B. Crawford
subfiles.about: Asks whether private correspondence with Japan had resumed and what censorship restrictions applied.
subfiles.summary: Crawford explains that he had corresponded with people in Japan before World War II and wished to resume writing. He asks for information about prohibited subjects so that his letters would not require deletions or appear noncompliant.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on permissible personal and business mail
subfiles.from: Harvey B. Otterman for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the principal censorship prohibitions affecting letters and postcards exchanged with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department says personal and business messages were generally acceptable but could not themselves transfer currency, checks, drafts, credit instruments, or evade controls on Japanese external assets. Certain patent, copyright, and media-rights communications were also restricted. Many business and financial messages were permissible if the actual transactions used approved channels, and Crawford was referred to his post office and the Army’s Civil Affairs Division for fuller guidance.

subfiles.title: Sebald despatch on commercial entrants’ censorship complaints
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports complaints that Occupation censorship delayed commercial mail and improperly disseminated confidential business information.
subfiles.summary: Commercial entrants alleged that information extracted from their correspondence was circulated within SCAP’s Economic and Scientific Section and sometimes reached competitors involved in import and export contracting. They also claimed censorship could lengthen New York–Tokyo airmail transit from two or three days to as many as ten. Sebald’s mission regarded dissemination of purely commercial intelligence as unethical and noted support within headquarters for lifting routine commercial-mail censorship, as well as informal agreement to exempt the American Chamber of Commerce in Japan’s organizational mail.

subfiles.title: Sebald despatch on relaxation of Occupation censorship
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Assesses reports that the Civil Censorship Detachment was being dismantled or sharply reduced.
subfiles.summary: Sebald encloses a Nippon Times article and says that, although unauthorized, it appeared substantially accurate, while cautioning that the reported November 11 closure date might be speculative. He reviews the transition from pre-publication to post-publication controls and distinguishes censorship from the Detachment’s continuing intelligence-gathering function. He expects postal surveillance, if retained, to become more selective through sampling and watchlisted correspondence, while noting uncertainty about telecommunications monitoring and the likely persistence of counterintelligence units in each prefecture.

subfiles.title: Nippon Times article on cuts in censorship personnel
subfiles.from: Frank L. White, Associated Press
subfiles.about: Reports large-scale dismissals and transfers from the Occupation’s Civil Censorship Detachment.
subfiles.summary: The article says several thousand American, foreign, and Japanese employees were affected, including more than 2,000 Japanese mail censors. Officials denied that censorship was being completely abolished and linked the reduction to General Douglas MacArthur’s personnel policy. Mail-censorship operations at Tokyo Central Post Office were reportedly to close on November 11, while other units operated at Nagoya, Osaka, Kyushu, and Hokkaido.

subfiles.title: Oenslager inquiry about Japanese mail and transit visits
subfiles.from: George Oenslager
subfiles.about: Asks whether letters exchanged with Japanese citizens were censored and how long transit visitors could remain in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Oenslager requests information on censorship of letters sent to Japanese residents and of letters sent by Japanese citizens to Americans. He also asks about the permitted duration of a transit visit to Japan. The date is inferred from the departmental file number and December 7 receipt stamp.

subfiles.title: State Department censorship-intelligence requirements for Japan
subfiles.from: Walter E. Jessop
subfiles.about: Provides the State Department’s detailed subject requirements for intelligence derived from civil-censorship intercepts.
subfiles.summary: The requirements range from internal conditions in Japan, Korea, and Southeast Asia to Japanese politics, labor, education, religion, science, civil liberties, media, international movements, commercial agreements, petroleum, peace-treaty questions, tariffs, and foreign commercial policy. Particular attention is given to Communist and anti-union activity, forced labor, cartels, patents, technology transfers, pricing arrangements, corporate changes, and trade correspondence. Jessop proposes a trial analysis of mail between Japan and Southeast Asia, organized around commodities, quantities, prices, payment, delivery, production problems, and raw-material needs. The Department supplied no names for the watchlist.

subfiles.title: Supplement to State Department censorship requirements
subfiles.from: Walter E. Jessop
subfiles.about: Adds new quarterly intelligence priorities for the Civil Censorship program in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The supplement requests intercepts concerning employer organizations and labor-law revision, Communist influence in Southeast Asia and its trade with Eastern Bloc states, democratic trends, Japanese associations, police, youth activity, and changing social patterns. Jessop again states that the Department had no names to add to the watchlist.

interest: The bundle is unusually valuable because it follows censorship across several distinct phases: wartime humanitarian messaging, early Occupation control, transfer of parcel inspection to Japanese authorities, exploitation of correspondence for intelligence, and eventual retrenchment. The prescribed Red Cross phrases and kana limits show how personal news was compressed into administratively manageable forms, while the 1948 intelligence requirements reveal the extraordinary breadth of subjects mined from intercepted mail. The Levi correspondence and Sebald’s report on commercial complaints provide particularly concrete examples of how censorship affected scientific exchange, atomic-energy policy, business competition, privacy, and postal speed. The presence of later 1949 documents beyond the nominal file-title dates also illustrates how decimal-file bundles could accumulate related material after their stated chronological range.
